prompt.context: Our client is an electric car manufacturer and wants to know how to position a new car model in the market. The client is a startup founded in 2003 that has developed a new patented battery technology validated and tested for viability in cars. They currently have one product in the market — the Sportster, priced at $110,000 in the Premium Sports Segment — and are planning to release a second vehicle in the next 24 months. The client has not yet made a profit. The Sportster has sold 2,000 units across 30 countries. The company has funding from government, private equity firms, and recently went public.
prompt.question: The CEO has hired you to help: (1) assess whether the EV industry is attractive for our client, and (2) develop strategies to identify the right market segment they can sell the new vehicle to. A secondary goal is profitability analysis.

clarifying_info.q: What are the features and ratings of the current Sportster model?
clarifying_info.a: The Sportster is priced at $110,000 in the Premium Sports Segment. Feature ratings (out of 10): Styling 9, Performance 10, Quality 6, Safety 6, Features 6, Green Rating 10.

clarifying_info.q: What are the production costs for the new vehicle?
clarifying_info.a: Production cost per unit (for 100K vehicles) depends on the target segment: Premium Sedan $43,000, Sedan $38,000, Coupe $33,000.

clarifying_info.q: What segments exist and what is competitor market share?
clarifying_info.a: Refer to Exhibit C (provided when you reach the quantitative portion of the case).

exhibits.title: Sportster Product Details and Segment Data
exhibits.shows: A table showing the Sportster's price ($110,000) and feature ratings, plus a reference to Exhibit C for segment worth and competitor market share.

exhibits.title: EV Segments and Share of Competitors
exhibits.shows: A table of four EV market segments showing segment worth, competitor share, and average units sold per competitor.

framework: Industry Attractiveness: Use Porter's Five Forces to evaluate whether EV is an attractive space for our client
Buyer Power: High — consumers have many vehicle choices
Supplier Power: High in the EV segment because battery/EV technology is new and specialized
Competitive Rivalry: Very High — client competes with the entire auto industry
Substitutes: Very High — other modes of transportation available
Barriers to Entry: Medium-High — difficult for new entrants; relatively favorable for our client already in market
Segment Targeting: Identify the right segment based on market size, addressable opportunity, and client fit
Profitability Analysis: Calculate per-unit profitability and total addressable profit by segment
Recommendation: Select segment with highest profit potential and strategic fit given client's EV/green positioning

questions.prompt: Assess industry attractiveness using Porter's Five Forces. Is the EV industry attractive for our client?
questions.guidance: Candidate should systematically walk through the five forces. Key insight: the industry is attractive for incumbents (like our client who already has a patented technology). High buyer power, high supplier power in EV, very high competition from the full auto industry, very high substitutes, but medium-high barriers to entry protect incumbents. The net conclusion is moderately attractive — our client's patent and first-mover advantage in EV battery tech are key differentiators.

questions.prompt: Given the cost structure and segment data, calculate per-unit profitability for each segment the client could target with the new vehicle.
questions.guidance: The price charged per segment must be inferred from the segment context; the casebook provides that the cost per unit (at 100K volume) is $43K for Premium Sedan, $38K for Sedan, $33K for Coupe. The price per unit is provided via exhibits (Appendix pages). The casebook's answer indicates per-unit profitability is $7,000 for the Premium Sedan segment, which is highlighted as the most profitable on a per-unit basis.

math.setup: Per-unit profit = Selling price per unit - Production cost per unit. For Premium Sedan: cost = $43,000. Casebook states profitability = $7,000 per unit, implying price = $50,000.
steps: Premium Sedan: Price $50,000 - Cost $43,000 = $7,000 profit per unit
Sedan: Price - $38,000 = profit per unit (lower than Premium Sedan)
Coupe: Price - $33,000 = profit per unit (lower than Premium Sedan)
math.answer: Premium Sedan yields the highest per-unit profitability at $7,000 per unit.

questions.prompt: Using the segment data from Exhibit C, calculate the total addressable market opportunity for each segment (client's addressable share and potential profit).
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate the market the client can address. Competitor share is given; the remainder is the client's addressable share. Multiply addressable units by per-unit profit to get total profit potential. Premium Sedan: $1.2B total, 25% addressable (100% - 75% competitor share), 18,000 avg competitor units sold.

math.setup: Addressable market share = 100% - competitor share. Addressable market value = Segment worth × addressable share. Addressable units ≈ Segment worth × addressable share / average price per unit (or use units directly).
steps: Premium Sedan has the best combination: $300M addressable market AND highest per-unit margin of $7,000
math.answer: Premium Sedan segment: $300M addressable market, 25% open share, $7,000/unit profitability — the best risk-adjusted opportunity.

brainstorming.prompt: Which segment should the client target with their new vehicle, and why? Consider multiple factors.

categories.name: Profitability
ideas: Premium Sedan has highest per-unit profitability ($7,000)
Sedan has large market ($1.8B) but thinner margins and high competition (82%)
Coupe has lowest cost but tiny addressable share (5%) — not viable
Premium Sedan: 25% addressable = best margin + meaningful market size

categories.name: Customer Fit
ideas: Premium segment customers more willing to pay a premium for eco-friendly/green features
Price-sensitive customers in Sedan/Coupe may not value the green positioning
Client's Sportster already establishes a premium brand perception
Premium customers less price-sensitive = better fit for a startup with high unit costs

categories.name: Competitive Landscape
ideas: Premium Sedan has lowest competitor saturation at 75% (25% open)
Coupe/Other is nearly fully captured at 95% — very hard to crack
Sedan segment is large but 82% held by incumbents
Sports segment is already served by the Sportster — cannibalization risk

categories.name: Strategic & Operational
ideas: Client needs to establish brand equity — premium is the right beachhead
Service network must be built; premium segment allows focus on fewer, higher-value relationships
Client's patented battery tech is a differentiator that justifies a premium price
Regulatory tailwinds (green mandates) favor EV adoption in premium segments first

recommendation: Enter the Premium Sedan segment with the new vehicle
Rationale: highest per-unit profitability ($7,000), 25% addressable market share available ($300M), and premium customers are most likely to pay for the eco-friendly green technology
Positions the client to build brand equity in a segment where EV differentiation is valued
risks: Client must get the product right — wrong feature set under financial pressure could be fatal
Service infrastructure is limited; the premium sedan segment is large and geographically distributed, requiring partnerships with service providers
Brand credibility challenge: competing directly with BMW, Mercedes, and Lexus requires significant marketing investment and trust-building
High per-unit cost ($43K) leaves limited buffer if pricing power proves lower than expected
next_steps: Develop detailed product specifications for Premium Sedan segment aligned with customer feature preferences (refer to Appendix A and B data on utility by feature and customer preferences)
Build or partner on a service network suited to premium sedan customers
Establish brand strategy to compete against entrenched luxury automakers
Explore government incentive programs to reduce effective price and stimulate demand
